claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from MNase-seq experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Cse4 hemisomes are immobile at centromeres.
claims.source: The stability of the Cse4 centromeric nucleosome and protection from background cleavages under these conditions confirm that Cse4 hemisomes are immobile at centromeres, as expected from the stability of Cse4 hemisomes on short DNA fragments, including a fragment consisting of CDEII alone (Figure 7B; Furuyama et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated based on protection from background cleavages and comparison to in vitro stability data.

claims.claim: The rotational and reflectional flexibility of the Cse4 nucleosome is attributable to the fact that a 78-bp CDEII duplex is sufficient to stably wrap a hemisome in vitro.
claims.source: We attribute this rotational and reflectional flexibility to the fact that a 78-bp CDEII duplex is sufficient to stably wrap a hemisome in vitro (Furuyama et al., 2013), and that AT-richness alone is sufficient for full in vivo function of CDEII, as some random 92% AT-rich sequences substituted for natural CDEII supported faithful segregation of mini-chromosomes (Baker and Rogers, 2005).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is stated with supporting citations to in vitro and in vivo studies.

claims.claim: Cbf1 acts as a barrier that sets the sharp rotational positions of the Cse4 nucleosomes that are asymmetrically oriented with H4S47 closest to CDEI.
claims.source: In addition, our findings suggest that Cbf1 acts as a barrier on the left that sets the sharp rotational positions of the Cse4 nucleosomes that are asymmetrically oriented with H4S47 closest to CDEI.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings regarding hemisome positioning.

claims.claim: Loss of Cbf1 is accompanied by a shift in position of the Cse4 nucleosome.
claims.source: This implied role of Cbf1 in Cse4 hemisome positioning is consistent with our previous analysis of MNase-seq data in a cbf1Δ mutant strain showing that loss of Cbf1 is accompanied by a shift in position of the Cse4 nucleosome (Krassovsky et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: The rotational and reflectional flexibility of the Cse4 nucleosome argues against specific roles for either Cbf1 or CBF3 in orienting the histone core within the single DNA wrap.
claims.source: The rotational and reflectional flexibility of the Cse4 nucleosome implied by our study argues against specific roles for either Cbf1 or CBF3 in orienting the histone core within the single DNA wrap (Xiao et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed flexibility in hemisome orientation and phasing.

claims.claim: Yeast strain Sby3 was used as control cells for cleavage mapping, MNase-seq and ChIP.
claims.source: Yeast strain Sby3 (MATa bar1-1 ura3-1 leu2, 3-112 his3-11 trp1-1 can1-100 ade2-1) was used as control cells for cleavage mapping, MNase-seq and ChIP as in our previous centromeric chromatin analysis (Krassovsky et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the experimental strains used.

claims.claim: H4S47C cells show growth anomalies relative to BY4741, which are caused by failure to achieve a quiescent state upon reaching stationary phase.
claims.source: As previously reported (Brogaard et al., 2012a), H4S47C cells show growth anomalies relative to BY4741, which we have determined are caused by failure to achieve a quiescent state upon reaching stationary phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation about the H4S47C strain with reference to a figure supplement.

claims.claim: The phenotypic syndrome of H4S47C is likely attributable to the replacement of the two histone H4 genes with a single mutant HHF1 gene, resulting in reduced H4 dosage.
claims.source: This phenotypic syndrome is likely attributable to the replacement of the two histone H4 genes, HHF1 and HHF2 with a single mutant HHF1 gene, resulting in reduced H4 dosage: Deleting HHF2 causes reduced starvation resistance (Davey et al., 2012), and partial histone depletion in general is associated with reduced longevity (Feser et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with supporting citations to related studies.

claims.claim: Sequencing data generated in this publication have been deposited with GEO (GSE51949).
claims.source: Sequencing data generated in this publication have been deposited with GEO (GSE51949, Henikoff et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Data availability section.

claims.claim: The cleavage pattern over centromeres is different from the large majority of cleavages on chromosome arms.
claims.source: However, the cleavage pattern over centromeres is different from the large majority of cleavages on chromosome arms.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the genome-wide cleavage mapping data.

claims.claim: No double peak pattern similar to that seen over centromeres was detected at the most frequently cleaved base pair on each chromosome.
claims.source: To test this possibility, we manually examined the region around the most frequently cleaved base pair on each chromosome (e.g., Figure 2E,G,I,K) but detected no double peak pattern similar to that seen over centromeres.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from manual examination of highly cleaved regions shown in figure panels.

claims.claim: For each chromosome, a centromere alignment to the profile scored above the best non-centromere alignment.
claims.source: For each chromosome, a centromere alignment to the profile (median r = 0.76) scored above the best non-centromere alignment (median r = 0.40) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from the profile scanning analysis shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: There was no consistent recovery bias seen for the single peaks of the most frequently cleaved base pair on every chromosome.
claims.source: In contrast, there was no consistent recovery bias seen for the single peaks of the most frequently cleaved base pair on every chromosome when similarly aligned (Figure 3B,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparison of centromeric and non-centromeric cleavage patterns shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Strong depletion is seen directly over the middle of aligned CDEIIs, gradually approaching 1 with distance from the mid-Cen.
claims.source: Strong depletion is seen directly over the middle of aligned CDEIIs, gradually approaching 1 with distance from the mid-Cen.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from normalized count analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: All 46 segments in the budding yeast genome that are at least 90% AT-rich over 83-bp are under-represented relative to expectation in the cleavage datasets.
claims.source: There are 46 segments in the budding yeast genome that are at least 90% AT-rich over 83-bp, the median length of CDEII, and all of them are under-represented relative to expectation in our cleavage datasets (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from analysis of AT-rich sequences shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The degree of representation decreases significantly with increasing AT-richness between 90–100%.
claims.source: Importantly, the degree of representation decreases significantly with increasing AT-richness between 90–100% (r = 0.52), showing depletions similar to what is seen for CDEII-containing fragments (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding with a correlation coefficient shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Similar 10-bp peak-to-peak distances within cleavage clusters were observed for all 16 centromeres.
claims.source: Similar 10-bp peak-to-peak distances within cleavage clusters were observed for all 16 centromeres, both for clusters on the left and on the right of the mid-Cen position.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the cleavage mapping data.

claims.claim: 10-bp spacings between H4S47C-anchored cleavages have previously been interpreted as differences in rotational phasing.
claims.source: Such 10-bp spacings between H4S47C-anchored cleavages have previously been interpreted as differences in rotational phasing (Brogaard et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a previous interpretation with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: The high-resolution crystal structure of the cenH3 octasome shows an arrangement of H4 residues that is virtually identical to that for the conventional H3 octasome.
claims.source: The high-resolution crystal structure of the cenH3 octasome shows an arrangement of H4 residues, including S47, that is virtually identical to that for the conventional H3 octasome (Tachiwana et al., 2011), and so would predict a similar cleavage pattern over the centromere as is seen for highly occupied and phased nucleosomes genome-wide.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: The minimal spacing of the inner cleavages is much larger than can be explained by the molecular dynamics model for a single nucleosome.
claims.source: This is clearly not the case at any yeast centromere, as even the minimal spacing of the inner cleavages is much larger than can be explained by our molecular dynamics model for a single nucleosome (Figure 1) or is observed for highly occupied and phased H3 nucleosomes throughout the genome (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing observed cleavage spacings to model predictions.

claims.claim: The presence of Scm3 as an integral part of the Cse4 nucleosome has been excluded based on subsequent in vivo mapping and in vitro reconstitution studies.
claims.source: The presence of Scm3 as an integral part of the Cse4 nucleosome has been excluded based on subsequent in vivo mapping (Shivaraju et al., 2011) and in vitro reconstitution studies (Cho and Harrison, 2011; Xiao et al., 2011), which leaves the hemisome as the only model that can account for the cleavage patterns that we observe.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from previous studies with supporting citations.

claims.claim: A model in which independent hemisomes align around the mid-Cen position in either orientation and in two rotational phases can account for all of the cleavage peaks observed over centromeres.
claims.source: Specifically, a model in which independent hemisomes align around the mid-Cen position in either orientation and in two rotational phases can account for all of the cleavage peaks that we observe over centromeres.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the structural model that explains the observed cleavage patterns.

claims.claim: Cen4 is 6–9 bp shorter than the other 15 centromeres.
claims.source: This ∼8-bp difference in cleavage pattern corresponds to the fact that, as pointed out above, Cen4 is 6–9 bp shorter than the other 15 centromeres.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation about centromere lengths.

claims.claim: The position of H4 residue 47 in the Cse4 core particle is fixed relative to the nearer junction regardless of whether the junction is CDEI-II or CDEII-III.
claims.source: A parsimonious explanation of this correspondence is that the position of H4 residue 47 in the Cse4 core particle is fixed relative to the nearer junction regardless of whether the junction is CDEI-II or CDEII-III.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the Cen4 cleavage pattern difference.

claims.claim: The 10-bp spacing between cleavage maxima implies that the rotational phase of the Cse4 nucleosome is established by where the nearer sequence-specific DNA-binding protein binds.
claims.source: In both cases, the 10-bp spacing between cleavage maxima implies that the rotational phase of the Cse4 nucleosome is established by where the nearer sequence-specific DNA-binding protein binds, whether it is Cbf1 at CDEI or the CBF3 complex at CDEIII.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the cleavage spacing patterns.

claims.claim: Peaks at −2, +5 and +12 were observed in the W-C distributions.
claims.source: We observed peaks at −2, +5 and +12 in the Watson-Crick (W-C) distributions (Figure 5A, red curve), which are all explained by the DNA positions shown to be accessible to H4S47C-phenanthroline-Cu+ in our structural model (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the W-C distance analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The +5 W-C peak results from cleavages by the same H4, whereas the −2 and +12 W-C peaks result from cleavages occurring on both sides of the dyad.
claims.source: The +5 W-C peak results from cleavages by the same H4, whereas the −2 and +12 W-C peaks result from cleavages occurring on both sides of the dyad.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on the structural model.

claims.claim: Genome-wide W-W' and C-C' distributions revealed strong peaks at +1 and +7.
claims.source: Their genome-wide distributions revealed strong peaks at +1 and +7 (Figure 5B,C red curves).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the distance analysis shown in Figure 5B,C.

claims.claim: The peak at +1 reflects cleavages due to the same H4 molecule on the same side of the dyad.
claims.source: The peak at +1 reflects cleavages due to the same H4 molecule on the same side of the dyad, while the peak at +7 reflects cleavages due to adjacent H4 molecules across the nucleosome dyad.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the W-W' and C-C' distance peaks.

claims.claim: A peak at +5 was observed in the W-C distribution for reads within 125 base-pairs of the center of CDEII, but peaks at −2 and +12 were not seen.
claims.source: Whereas we observed a peak at +5, which can arise from the presence of a single H4, the peaks at −2 and +12, which require two H4s on either side of the dyad axis, were not seen.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the centromere-specific W-C distribution analysis.

claims.claim: For the W–W' and C–C' distributions at centromeres, a strong peak at +1 was observed, whereas the peak at +7 was absent.
claims.source: For the W–W' and C–C' distributions we again observed a strong peak at +1 (Figure 5B,C, black curves), which can arise from a single H4, whereas the peak at +7, which results from cleavage across a dyad axis, was absent.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the centromere-specific distance analysis shown in Figure 5B,C.

claims.claim: The 10-bp peak spacing evident in the centromere maps is attributable to rotational phasing.
claims.source: Rather, the 10-bp peak spacing evident in the centromere maps (Figure 4) and attributable to rotational phasing was a prominent feature in both W–W' and C–C' for centromeres, but not genome-wide.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation and interpretation of the distance distributions.

claims.claim: The absence of peaks representing H4S47C-anchored cleavages across the dyad axis provides independent confirmation that single H4-containing particles predominate at centromeres.
claims.source: Taken together, the absence of peaks representing H4S47C-anchored cleavages across the dyad axis but the presence of peaks representing a single H4 at centromeres provides independent confirmation based on mapping of cleavage positions that single H4-containing particles predominate at centromeres.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated based on the distance distribution analysis.

claims.claim: The midpoints of the vertical lines of dots marking the preferred cleavages are precisely centered over the position of maximum occupancy of the Cse4 nucleosome.
claims.source: Finally, when log2(Cse4/Input) ChIP-seq profiles are superimposed over the V-plots, we see that the midpoints of the vertical lines of dots marking the preferred cleavages are precisely centered over the position of maximum occupancy of the Cse4 nucleosome.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the V-plot analysis with superimposed ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The very low level of cleavages observed over centromeres in wild-type cells confirms that centromere cleavage patterns are specific for H4S47C.
claims.source: The very low level of cleavages observed over centromeres (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) confirms that centromere cleavage patterns are specific for H4S47C and not for centromere-specific DNA-binding proteins.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the wild-type control experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The level of background cleavage over centromeres is similarly low regardless of whether or not cells were subjected to OP-labeling and cleavage reactions.
claims.source: This revealed that the level of background cleavage over centromeres is similarly low regardless of whether or not cells were subjected to OP-labeling and cleavage reactions, as expected if centromeres are fully occupied and protected during the cleavage reaction (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the background cleavage control experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: CenH3 nucleosomes are hypersensitive to MNase digestion in vivo.
claims.source: CenH3 nucleosomes are hypersensitive to MNase digestion in vivo (Takahashi et al., 1992; Dalal et al., 2007; Krassovsky et al., 2012), and some authors have suggested that hemisomes might represent unstable intermediates in the assembly or disassembly of octasomes (Black and Cleveland, 2011; Dunleavy et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Mapping of Cse4 hemisomes over centromeres at levels expected for such high AT-rich sequences implies that they are stable particles in vivo.
claims.source: Therefore, our mapping of Cse4 hemisomes over centromeres at levels expected for such high AT-rich sequences (Figure 3E) implies that they are stable particles in vivo as we previously showed for hemisomes wrapped by CDEII in vitro (Furuyama et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed occupancy levels with reference to previous in vitro work.

claims.claim: No changes in particle migration associated with the OP-labeling procedure were observed for any of the reconstituted octasomes.
claims.source: Using a gel-shift assay, we observed no changes in particle migration associated with the OP-labeling procedure for any of the reconstituted octasomes (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the gel-shift assay shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: OP-treated and untreated Cse4 and H3 octasomes are similar in height to one another but are ∼40–50% taller than Cse4-H4S47C/CDEII hemisomes.
claims.source: We found that OP-treated and untreated Cse4 and H3 octasomes are similar in height to one another but are ∼40–50% taller than Cse4-H4S47C/CDEII hemisomes reconstituted and incubated in parallel (Figure 7B), consistent with previous studies (Furuyama et al., 2013; Codomo et al., 2014; Walkiewicz et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from AFM analysis shown in Figure 7B with supporting citations.

claims.claim: CDEI, CDEII and CDEIII are strongly MNase-protected relative to flanking regions in both strains with or without OP treatment in both soluble and insoluble chromatin fractions.
claims.source: In both cases, midpoint V-plots reveal that CDEI, CDEII and CDEIII are strongly MNase-protected relative to flanking regions in both strains with or without OP treatment in both soluble and insoluble chromatin fractions.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from MNase-seq V-plot analysis of different chromatin fractions.

claims.claim: The extent of Cse4 particle occupancy is half that necessary to accommodate two spaced hemisomes.
claims.source: This extent of Cse4 particle occupancy is half that necessary to accommodate two spaced hemisomes, because if the cleavage pairs were attributable to two hemisomes particles wrapping ∼60 bp with spacings of 33–53 bp between cleavage sites, then the total span would be 153–173 bp, or about twice the ∼80 bp that the Cse4-containing particle occupies.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a calculation-based inference from the observed occupancy and cleavage patterns.

claims.claim: The single hemisome per centromere model is the only one that can account for the cleavage data.
claims.source: This leaves the single hemisome per centromere model as the only one that can account for our cleavage data.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated after ruling out alternative models based on occupancy calculations.

claims.claim: The hydroxy radical cleavage protocol was originally developed for mapping non-specific cleavages within linker DNA.
claims.source: As the hydroxy radical cleavage protocol that we use was originally developed for mapping non-specific cleavages within linker DNA (Cartwright and Elgin, 1982), these diagonals indicate a moderate level of background cleavage between flanking highly occupied and phased nucleosomes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as background information about the cleavage method with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Fragile nucleosomes are thought to be unstable based on hypersensitivity to MNase.
claims.source: We also observed background cleavages at sites of 'fragile' nucleosomes, which are thought to be unstable based on hypersensitivity to MNase (Xi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: There was no evidence of nucleosome-directed cleavage at the Gal4 UAS, but rather especially strong cleavage diagonals directly over the Gal4 UAS.
claims.source: However, there was no evidence of nucleosome-directed cleavage, but rather especially strong cleavage diagonals directly over the Gal4 UAS (UASg, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the cleavage analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: The 'X' pattern of depletion seen at fragile nucleosome sites resembles that for known nucleosome depleted regions.
claims.source: The 'X' pattern of depletion seen at these sites resembles that for known nucleosome depleted regions, such as those around binding sites for the Reb1 and Abf1 transcription factors (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparison to known nucleosome-depleted regions shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Centromeres showed very little cleavage relative to regions on either side, indicating protection from background cleavages.
claims.source: In contrast, centromeres showed very little cleavage relative to regions on either side (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), indicating protection from background cleavages and confirming that Cse4 nucleosome-directed cleavages depend on the H4S47C mutation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the wild-type control experiment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The stability of the Cse4 centromeric nucleosome and protection from background cleavages confirm that Cse4 hemisomes are immobile at centromeres.
claims.source: The stability of the Cse4 centromeric nucleosome and protection from background cleavages under these conditions confirm that Cse4 hemisomes are immobile at centromeres, as expected from the stability of Cse4 hemisomes on short DNA fragments, including a fragment consisting of CDEII alone (Figure 7B; Furuyama et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is stated based on multiple lines of evidence including protection from cleavage and comparison to in vitro data.

results.result: Molecular dynamics simulations predict that H4S47C-phenanthroline-Cu+ can contact DNA at specific positions near the nucleosome dyad and catalyze double-strand cleavages.
results.evaluation: Claims C30 and C31 describe molecular dynamics simulation results showing copper contacts at specific DNA positions and the inference that single H4S47C-phenanthroline-Cu+ can catalyze double-strand cleavages. The simulation data is presented in Figure 1B and the inference is logically derived from contacts on both DNA strands.

results.result: H4S47C-anchored cleavage mapping is an unbiased, endonucleolytic method that reveals precise H4 positions and can distinguish between symmetrical and asymmetrical nucleosome structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C21, C26, and C27 collectively describe the capabilities and advantages of the H4S47C-anchored cleavage mapping method. These are supported by methodological descriptions, citations to prior work (C21), and comparisons to MNase (C26). The ability to distinguish structural models (C27) is a stated advantage that is subsequently tested.

results.result: The H4S47C mutant strain shows normal centromere function with identical doubling times and plasmid retention rates, though it exhibits growth anomalies in stationary phase attributable to reduced H4 dosage.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C54, and C55 describe the phenotype of the H4S47C strain. C33 reports normal centromere function based on growth and plasmid retention data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). C54 and C55 acknowledge stationary phase defects and attribute them to reduced H4 dosage with supporting citations. The data support that the mutation does not impair centromere function during the experimental conditions used.

results.result: Centromeres display a unique cleavage pattern consisting of two clusters spaced ~40 bp apart that is not found elsewhere in the genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C34, C35, C57, C58, and C59 collectively establish the uniqueness of the centromere cleavage pattern. The pattern is described (C34), shown to differ from chromosome arms (C57), not found at other highly cleaved sites (C58), and validated by exhaustive genome-wide scanning with statistical correlation analysis (C59, Table 1). The evidence strongly supports the uniqueness claim.

results.result: Biased recovery of CDEII-containing fragments is attributable to their high AT-richness (>90%), as demonstrated by similar depletion of other AT-rich sequences in the genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 and C60-C63 describe the fragment recovery bias and its attribution to AT-richness. The bias is observed at centromeres (C36) but not at other highly cleaved sites (C60). The AT-richness explanation is supported by analysis of all 46 genomic regions ≥90% AT-rich (C62) showing correlation between AT-richness and depletion (C63, r=0.52). This provides strong evidence for the AT-richness explanation.

results.result: High-resolution cleavage mapping reveals that each centromere cluster resolves into pairs separated by ~10 bp, with inner peaks 33 bp apart and outer peaks 53 bp apart for most centromeres, interpreted as rotational phasing differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 and C64-C65 describe the fine structure of centromere cleavage patterns. The 10-bp spacing is observed for all 16 centromeres (C64), the 33/53 bp spacing is measured from composite alignments (C39), and Cen4 shows different spacing corresponding to its shorter length (C40). The interpretation as rotational phasing (C65) is supported by prior citation. The data are internally consistent and well-documented in Figure 4.

results.result: The observed cleavage patterns at centromeres are incompatible with octameric nucleosomes and (Cse4/H4)2 tetrasomes based on comparison to the molecular dynamics model and genome-wide nucleosome patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C28, C41, C66, and C67 collectively argue against octasome and tetrasome models. The argument is based on: (1) the crystal structure predicting similar H4 arrangements in octasomes (C66), (2) the observed spacing being much larger than predicted by the molecular dynamics model (C67), and (3) symmetrical structures being incompatible with the observed asymmetric patterns (C28, C41). The logic is sound and supported by the structural modeling and cleavage data.

results.result: Each yeast centromere is occupied by oppositely oriented Cse4/H4/H2A/H2B hemisomes in two rotational phases, representing the only structural model compatible with the cleavage data.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C29, C42, C43, C68, and C69 present the hemisome model as the conclusion. After ruling out octasomes, tetrasomes (C4, C5, C28, C41), and Scm3-containing particles (C68), the hemisome model is presented as the only compatible structure (C42, C69). The model accounts for all observed cleavage peaks (C69) and explains the rotational flexibility (C43). The logic is sound given the exclusion of alternative models.

results.result: Watson-Crick and same-strand distance distributions confirm that single H4-containing particles predominate at centromeres, as peaks requiring two H4s across the dyad are absent at centromeres but present genome-wide.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C80 describe the distance distribution analysis. Genome-wide patterns show peaks at positions requiring two H4s (C73-C76), while centromere patterns show only peaks consistent with single H4 (C77-C78). The 10-bp rotational phasing is prominent at centromeres (C79). The conclusion that single H4-containing particles predominate (C80) is well-supported by the absence of cross-dyad peaks at centromeres. This provides independent confirmation of the hemisome model.

results.result: Centromere-specific hemisomes are inferred from distances observed between closely-spaced H4 cleavages, providing independent confirmation of single H4-containing particles.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C45 state that hemisome structure is inferred from cleavage distances. This is supported by the detailed distance distribution analysis (C73-C80) showing absence of cross-dyad peaks at centromeres. The claim that this provides independent confirmation (C45) is justified as it uses a different analytical approach (distance distributions) from the direct cleavage pattern analysis.

results.result: OP-labeling does not alter nucleosome structure, as demonstrated by gel-shift assays, AFM measurements, and MNase-seq showing identical Cse4 nucleosome positions in treated and untreated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C46, C47, C86, and C87 address concerns about OP-labeling artifacts. Multiple independent methods confirm no structural changes: gel-shift shows no migration changes (C86), AFM shows octasomes remain taller than hemisomes (C87), and MNase-seq shows identical positioning (C47). The convergence of evidence from multiple techniques strongly supports the conclusion (C46).

results.result: Cse4 hemisomes are stable and immobile at centromeres in vivo, as evidenced by protection from background cleavages and recovery at expected levels for AT-rich sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C82, C83, C84, C85, C95, and C96 address hemisome stability. Despite prior reports of MNase hypersensitivity (C84), the mapping at expected levels for AT-rich sequences (C85) and protection from background cleavages (C82, C83, C95) support stability. The conclusion (C48, C96) is supported by multiple lines of evidence including comparison to in vitro data (cited in C48, C96).

results.result: V-plot analysis combined with ChIP-seq and MNase-seq confirms that cleavages are centered over Cse4 occupancy and that the particle occupancy is consistent with a single hemisome per centromere rather than two spaced hemisomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C81, C88, C89, and C90 describe V-plot analysis integrating multiple data types. The alignment of cleavages with Cse4 ChIP peaks (C81), MNase protection of CDEI-II-III (C88), and calculation showing occupancy is half that needed for two hemisomes (C89) converge to support the single hemisome model (C90). The quantitative argument in C89 is particularly strong.

results.result: The orientation and rotational position of hemisomes is not specified by the centromere sequence but is influenced by proximity to DNA-binding proteins (Cbf1 or CBF3), with Cbf1 acting as a barrier setting rotational positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C49-C52, and C70-C72 address hemisome positioning determinants. The flexibility in orientation/phase (C8, C49) is attributed to AT-richness being sufficient for wrapping (C49, with citations). The Cen4 difference (C70-C72) suggests positioning relative to nearer junction. Cbf1's role as barrier (C50) is supported by prior cbf1Δ data (C51). However, the flexibility argues against specific orientation roles (C52). The evidence supports the main conclusion but some aspects are interpretive.

results.result: Background cleavages occur at nucleosome-depleted regions and fragile nucleosomes, as demonstrated by analysis of the Gal4 UAS and other sites showing 'X' patterns characteristic of depleted regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 characterize background cleavages. The hydroxy radical method's known properties (C91) and the observation of strong diagonals at the Gal4 UAS (C93) and fragile nucleosomes (C92) showing 'X' patterns (C94) are consistent. This helps distinguish nucleosome-directed cleavages from background and validates the interpretation of centromere protection.
